hero.title: Supreme Court: Chief Justice of India
hero.description: Master the constitutional framework of the Supreme Court of India and the office of the Chief Justice of India (Articles 124 to 147)—including appointment processes, the Collegium System, removal procedure, independence guarantees, and jurisdictions (GS Paper-II: Indian Polity).

mockIntro.title: Interactive UPSC Mock Test
mockIntro.description: Evaluate your understanding of Articles 124-147, Collegium Cases, Judges Inquiry Act, and SC Jurisdictions (Original, Appellate, Writ, Advisory).

timeline.title: Historical Evolution of Judicial Appointments
timeline.description: The evolution of the judicial appointment process through key landmark cases.

cards.details: Supreme Court ruled that 'consultation' does not mean 'concurrence' of the Chief Justice. It gave the executive primacy in judicial appointments.
SC reversed its 1981 ruling, declaring that 'consultation' means 'concurrence'. Established the Collegium System consisting of the CJI and 2 senior-most judges.
On a Presidential reference (Article 143), the SC expanded the Collegium to a 5-member body consisting of the CJI and 4 senior-most associate judges.
The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act as unconstitutional, reviving the Collegium System.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Memory aids to retain Supreme Court Articles and jurisdictions.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Remember that Article 124 is the foundational article detailing the establishment, composition, and appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court.

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Remember Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a 'Court of Record' with power to punish for contempt of itself.

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: Remember 131 is for Original Jurisdiction (federal disputes between Centre vs. States or State vs. State, one-on-one).

items.title: Mnemonic 4
items.decryption: Remember 143 (which has 1, 4, 3 letters like 'I Love You') is the President seeking advice/consultation from the Supreme Court.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Active-recall review of judicial appointments, jurisdictions, and removal.

items.question: What is the minimum age prescribed in the Constitution for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge?
items.answer: None. The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum age for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court. It only lays down qualifications (citizen, 5 years HC judge, or 10 years HC advocate, or distinguished jurist).

items.question: What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court Judge?
items.answer: A Supreme Court judge holds office until they attain the age of 65 years (Article 124(2)).

items.question: Can the salaries of Supreme Court Judges be reduced during their tenure?
items.answer: No. Under Article 125(2), their salaries, allowances, and privileges cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment, except during a Financial Emergency (Article 360).

items.question: Is the advisory opinion given by the Supreme Court under Article 143 binding on the President?
items.answer: No. The opinion is advisory only. The President is free to follow or ignore it, as decided in multiple landmark reference cases.

items.question: What constitutes a 'Court of Record' under Article 129?
items.answer: It means: (1) The judgments, proceedings, and acts of the Supreme Court are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony (evidential value in all courts), and (2) It has the power to punish for contempt of itself (fine or imprisonment).

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Believing a citizen can file a writ petition directly in the Supreme Court for violation of ordinary legal rights. No! Article 32 writ jurisdiction can only be invoked for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. For other legal rights, one must go to High Courts under Article 226.

Trap 2: Assuming the impeachment of a Supreme Court Judge is completed entirely by Parliament. The removal motion must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3rd present and voting) during the same session, but the final removal order is issued by the President.

Trap 3: Confusing the scope of Original Jurisdiction under Article 131. It does NOT cover: (1) Disputes arising out of pre-constitution treaties, (2) Inter-state water disputes (which go to separate tribunals under Article 262), and (3) Ordinary disputes between a citizen and the Centre/State.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Comprehensive structured analysis of the Supreme Court of India.

sections.title: 1. Appointment, Collegium & Removal
sections.content:
Appointment of Judges (Article 124)

Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President. For appointment of the CJI, the President consults such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as he deems necessary (by convention, the senior-most judge of the SC is appointed). For other judges, consultation with the CJI is mandatory. The 'consultation' process is governed by the Collegium system, which requires consensus from a 5-member body.

Removal Procedure (Judges Inquiry Act, 1968):

  • Grounds: Proved misbehavior or incapacity (Article 124(4)).
  • Motion: Must be signed by 100 members in Lok Sabha or 50 members in Rajya Sabha. Admitted by Speaker/Chairman.
  • Investigation: A 3-member committee (SC Judge, HC CJ, distinguished jurist) investigates.
  • Passage: Passed in both Houses by a special majority in the same session. Final removal order issued by the President.

sections.title: 2. Jurisdictions & Constitutional Powers
sections.content:
Jurisdictional Framework of the Apex Court

The Supreme Court of India has wider jurisdiction than most national courts. It is a federal court, a court of appeal, a protector of fundamental rights, and an advisory body to the executive. Its decisions are binding on all courts under Article 141.

Jurisdiction typeConstitutional Scope
Original (Art 131)Federal disputes between Centre and States, or States amongst themselves. Excludes private disputes.
Writ (Art 32)Original but concurrent with High Court (Art 226) for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Appellate (Art 132-136)Appeals in Constitutional, Civil, Criminal, and Special Leave Petition (SLP) cases.
Advisory (Art 143)Opinion sought by the President. Non-binding advisory jurisdiction.

sections.title: 3. Independence of Judiciary & Judicial Review
sections.content:
Constitutional Guarantees of Independence

To maintain the rule of law, the Constitution safeguards judicial independence: (1) Security of tenure (removal requires special parliamentary address), (2) Fixed service conditions, (3) Expenses charged on Consolidated Fund of India (not voted on by Parliament), (4) Prohibition on discussion of conduct of judges in Parliament (Article 121), and (5) Ban on practice after retirement (Article 124(7)).

Judicial Review & Article 137

The Supreme Court has the power of Judicial Review (reviewing legislative acts and executive orders against the Constitution). Under Article 137, the Supreme Court also has the power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by itself, allowing it to reverse its own decisions (e.g., Kesavananda Bharati case reversing Golaknath case).
